segments.source: Which is older, Layer C or Layer B? Can the exact year of deposition of Layer A be deduced? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

1. C lies below B, so C is older than B by the stratigraphic rule. 2. No exact dated object or deposition year is given for A. 3. Therefore only relative ordering, not an exact year for A, is justified. Cross-domain check: 2×2=4 km.
Layer C is older than Layer B. The exact deposition year of Layer A cannot be deduced. Cross-domain answer: 4 km.
Relative dating and absolute dating answer different questions and should not be confused.
Partial order from vertical position plus numeric constraints from dated objects.
Problem 841. Applying a rule with an exception: Maya
Rules often have conditions and exceptions. Logical reading prevents us from applying a general rule when an overriding exception is active.

Maya is 13 years old. A library rule says: a child may enter the archive room if age ≥ 14 AND an adult permit is present. Exception: during an evacuation drill, nobody may enter. Permit present: yes. Evacuation drill: no.
Check exceptions first if they override the general rule. Otherwise every condition joined by AND must be true.
May Maya enter the archive room under these facts? Show which conditions succeed or fail.
1. Age test: 13≥14 is False. 2. Permit test is True. 3. Because the general rule uses AND, both tests must pass. 4. Therefore entry is not allowed.
The order of reasoning matters when exceptions override ordinary rules.
Boolean rule with priority: exception predicate first, then conjunction of eligibility conditions.

C2. Rights as limits on decisions
Problem 846. Majority rule and a protected right: case 1
Democratic procedures use voting, but constitutional systems can place some rights beyond ordinary majority power.

A council of 21 members votes 16 to 5 for a proposal that would forbid one named group from the right to speak at a peaceful meeting. The classroom constitution states: (1) ordinary proposals pass by simple majority; (2) an ordinary majority may not remove the listed equal rights from a group.
A decision must satisfy both the voting procedure and the higher rights constraint. Passing a vote is not sufficient if the content violates a protected right.
Did the proposal receive a majority? May it take effect under the stated constitution?

1. Vote check: 16>5, so the proposal has a simple majority. 2. Content check: the proposal removes a protected equal right (speak at a peaceful meeting) from a group. 3. The higher rights rule therefore blocks the proposal even though the vote passed.
It received a majority, but it may not take effect under the stated rights rule.
A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.
Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.
